summary.text: Seven-gated Thebes of Cadmus and Oedipus — the Boeotian city whose royal house was torn apart by curse, fratricide, and the war of the Seven; its Epigon king Thersander sailed for Troy but fell to Telephus in Mysia before the host reached Ilion.
Rich Orchomenos of the Minyae — the Boeotian kingdom whose kings Clymenus and Erginus once laid tribute on Thebes until Heracles broke their host and Megara was given as the victor's prize.
Rich in gold, Mycenae of the Lion Gate — Agamemnon's citadel and the mustering seat of the Achaean host against Troy.

Midea on the eastern Argive plain — the citadel Perseus fortified beside Mycenae and Tiryns when he exchanged Argos for Megapenthes' kingdom; Pausanias places it on the road from Tiryns toward Epidaurus.

Argos of Danaus and Perseus — the Peloponnesian kingdom whose kings mustered the Seven against Thebes, sent Diomedes with the largest Argive contingent to Troy, and held the oldest claim to Hera's favour.
Athena's olive-crowned city — Cecrops' ancient acropolis, Theseus' united Attica, and the Attic hearth of the Ionian migration.
Sparta of Tyndareus' house — Menelaus' kingdom and Helen's home, from whose wronged hearth the Achaeans sailed to Troy.
Sandy Pylos of the Neleids — Neleus' kingdom on the Messenian coast, where old Nestor counselled the Achaeans and mustered ninety ships to Troy.

Andania of the Great Goddesses — Polycaon and Messene founded it and built their palace here; Caucon first taught the mysteries on this spot, and Lycus son of Pandion later brought the full Attic rite when exiled from Athens.
Before Aphareus founded Arene, Perieres and the earlier Messenian kings dwelt at Andania — the inland seat from which the Aeolid line held the country until the coastward courts moved seaward.

Lovely Arene of the Apharetids — Aphareus' Messenian city, named for his wife, whence Idas and keen-eyed Lynceus sailed to the Argo; Homer counts it in Nestor's kingdom beside sandy Pylos, where the Minyeius flows into the sea.

Pausanias could not fix the ruins in his own day and reports that many held heroic Arene identical with Samicum on the Triphylian coast — the map point follows Pleiades' Samikon entry under that disputed identification.
Ilion of Priam on the Trojan plain — the besieged city whose fall Homer sang, and whose ashes seeded the wanderings of the survivors.
Corinth of the Isthmus — the wealthy crossroads polis whose kings Sisyphus and Glaucus belong to the oldest tales of cunning, and from whose harbour the Argonauts once put to sea.

After Pelias, Jason and Medea lived ten years at Corinth until Creon's daughter Glauce drew the hero away — and the witch answered with fire; elsewhere Polybus and Periboea raised the exposed Oedipus, and Peirene's spring still marks the gateway to the city.
Tiryns of the Cyclopean walls — the fortress Proetus built, Perseus took in exchange for Argos, and where Heracles served Eurystheus at the start of his labours.
Nauplia on the Argive coast — the port Nauplius son of Poseidon and Amymone founded, with Poseidon's sanctuary, harbours, and the spring Canathus where the Argives say Hera bathes each year.

Temenium on the upper Argolic gulf — fifty stades from Nauplia, named for Temenus who fortified it as his base in the Dorian Return before taking Argos; Pausanias saw Poseidon's and Aphrodite's temples and Temenus' tomb.
Megara on the Saronic coast — the city of Nisus and Scylla, where Alcathous rebuilt the walls and where Perseus went down to reign after the death of Acrisius.
Telamon's island kingdom in the Saronic Gulf — home of the greater Ajax and Teucer, who led the Salaminians beside the Athenian host at Troy.
Aeacus' island in the Saronic Gulf — where Zeus carried off the nymph Aegina, raised ants into the Myrmidons, and the pious king kept the keys of Hades after death.
Knossos of Minos — the Cretan palace-city whose labyrinth held the Minotaur and whose king's thalassocracy Homer knew when Odysseus saw him judging the dead.
Iolcus on the Pagasetic gulf — Pelias' citadel in Thessaly, whence Jason was sent forth for the fleece; Apollonius sets the heroes' assembly and the Argo's launch at Pagasae on the harbour below.
Homer's Catalogue of Ships names well-built Iolcus beside Pherae, Boebe, and Glaphyrae on lake Boebeis — towns whose spearmen followed Eumelus son of Admetus with eleven black ships to Troy.
Larissa of the Thessalian plain — Pirithous' city of the Lapiths, and the Pelasgian kingdom where Teutamides held funeral games when Perseus' quoit fulfilled the oracle.

Pherae beside lake Boebeis — the city Pheres founded in Thessaly, where Apollo served Admetus as herdsman and Alcestis died in her husband's stead; in the Catalogue of Ships Eumelus son of Admetus led eleven black ships from the Pheraean quarter of the host.

Boebe on the eastern shore of lake Boebeis — Magnesian town named in the Catalogue of Ships beside Pherae, Glaphyrae, and well-built Iolcus, whose spearmen followed Eumelus son of Admetus with eleven black ships.

Glaphyrae in Magnesian Thessaly — settlement beside lake Boebeis named with Pherae, Boebe, and Iolcus in Eumelus' muster roll, when the dear son of Admetus led eleven ships from the Pheraean quarter of the host.
Chalcis on the Euripus — chief city of the Abantes, whose prince Elephenor son of Chalcodon led the island's host to Troy.
Cerinthus on Euboea — the city whence Canthus the Argonaut sailed, fated never to return once Apollo's oracle ordained his death in Libya.
Gortyn on Crete's southern plain — the cliff-girt city beside the misty deep where Menelaus' storm-tossed ships scraped the headland on the road home from Troy.
The kingdom at the eastern edge of the Greek world — Aea of Aeëtes, where the fleece hung in the sacred grove and Jason's Argonauts won Medea by the king's own trial.
Semiramis' eastern Babylon — where Ovid sets the adjoining houses of Pyramus and Thisbe by the queen's brick walls, and where their blood darkened the mulberry beside Ninus' tomb.
Bebrycia on the Propontis shore — kingdom of King Amycus, son of Poseidon and a Bithynian nymph, who forced every stranger to box and was slain by Polydeuces when the Argonauts landed.
Mariandyni on the Propontis shore — kingdom of King Lycus, who welcomed the Argonauts after Polydeuces slew Amycus; there Idmon was gored by a boar and Tiphys died of illness.
The white-walled capital of Egypt — where Io wandered as a cow under Hera's gadfly, where Proteus kept his shifting shapes, and where Helen was said to have sat out the Trojan War in phantom form.
Syracuse on Ortygia — the Corinthian colony Delphi sent Archias to found, where the oracle said the mouth of Alpheus would mingle with broad Arethusa's springs on the misty island facing Trinacria.
The great Sicilian city stood at the western horizon of the Greek world — refuge of Daedalus after Icarus fell, and the shore toward which Odysseus' long wandering touched the Italian West.

Lavinium on the Laurentine coast — where Apollodorus and Hyginus send Aeneas after Troy among the Italian peoples, the Latin landing of the Dardanian line that the Returns count among the wanderers who reached the West.
Ovid names Lavinium's sacred homes on the Tiber approach and sets Aeneas' washing in the Numicius at the Laurentine shore before the hero passes into the god Indiges.
Liguria on the Eridanus — where King Cycnus, kinsman and lover of Phaethon, left his peopled cities and throne to mourn among the Heliades' poplars until grief remade him a swan.
Cumae on the Campanian marsh — first Greek colony on the Italian mainland, where Trojan Aeneas landed, sacrificed, and begged the long-lived Sibyl for passage to Avernus and his father's shade.
Pausanias knew Cumae among the Opici as the home of Sibyls — Demo of Cumae and the stone urn in Apollo's sanctuary said to hold the Sibyl's bones.

Tarentum on the heel of Italy — Spartan colony of Phalanthus, whom Delphi's oracle sent to seize the coast when rain fell from a cloudless sky upon his wife Aethra's tears, and named for Taras son of Poseidon.
The Tarentines dedicated spoils and horse-offerings at Olympia and Delphi — a flagship city of Achaean Magna Graecia where hero cult and colonial myth met the wider Greek world.
Croton on the Ionian coast — Spartan colony sent with Locri under Polydorus, and in Crotonian legend the starting-point of Leonymus' voyage to the White Island where Achilles received hero cult.
Ovid tells how Hercules rested at far-famed Croton and promised the place to Myscelus' race; the city that bears Croton's buried bones still keeps his name on the Italian shore.
Locri by the Western headland — Spartan colony paired with Croton when Polydorus sent settlers across the sea, the Epizephyrian city on the toe of Italy.
The Locrians who dwell near the Western Cape dedicated a gilded boxwood Apollo at Olympia — Patrocles of Croton made the image that Pausanias saw among the hero offerings.

Rhegium on the Calabrian shore — opposite Zancle across the strait where Homer set Scylla and Charybdis, and the crossing Heracles used when a bull swam from Rhegium to Sicily and gave Italy its name.
Ovid sets Galatea's tale beside the opposite walls of Rhegium and the sea abundant in shipwreck — the Ausonian shore facing Sicily across the Tyrrhenian passage.
The navel of the earth — Apollo's oracle on the slopes of Parnassus, where the Pythia spoke for gods and kings and the temple treasury held the tribute of Greece.
The Altis of Zeus — sanctuary of the Olympic games, where Pelops won Hippodamia and the victors' olive crowns were cut from the god's sacred grove.
The Telesterion of Demeter — where the Mysteries were celebrated, Persephone returned from the underworld, and initiates walked the Sacred Way from Athens.
The oak of Zeus at Dodona — oldest oracle in Greece, where the god spoke in the rustle of sacred leaves and the bronze cauldrons chimed when the wind struck them.
Nemea of the lion — where Heracles strangled the beast at the start of his labours, and where the Nemean games were founded in honour of the dead child Opheltes.
Vine-clad Epidaurus of the Argolid — a Homeric city in Diomedes' muster, and later the kingdom Deiphontes and Hyrnetho held when the Heraclids took the land from Argos.
The sanctuary of Asclepius at Epidaurus — the healing god's greatest shrine, where the sick slept in the abaton and woke cured by the serpent-god's dream.
The Brauronian Artemis — where young Athenian girls served the goddess as arktoi, the little bears, in rites of passage beside the marshy stream.
The Isthmian sanctuary of Poseidon — beside the Corinthian crossing, where the games in honour of the sea-god drew Greeks from every quarter of the Peloponnese.

Apollodorus says Sisyphus founded the Isthmian games for Melicertes after Ino's sea-leap; Pausanias tells how the boy was borne ashore here by a dolphin, buried by Sisyphus on the Isthmus, and honoured thereafter as Palaemon — while sailors invoke his mother Leucothea beside the crossing.
Holy Delos — the Cycladic isle where Leto bore Apollo and Artemis, Asteria's quail-form become stone, and Anius son of Apollo ruled the Delian city when Aeneas came to Apollo's shore.
The sacred isle of Delos — birthplace of Apollo and Artemis, where Leto found refuge and the Delian league later centred its treasury.

Claros of Colophon — Apollo's oracular shrine beside the sea, named with Delphi and Patara when the god walked among mortals and when Jason passed through the Ionian coast; near Notium where Calchas died after Mopsus outprophesied him.
Samothrace — the North Aegean island whose wooded peak Homer gave Poseidon as a seat overlooking Ida and Troy, and from which Dardanus sailed after Iasion's death.
Sea-girt Naxos — the Cycladic isle Homer calls Dia, where Theseus left Ariadne and Dionysus found her, and where Artemis slew the Cretan princess on the god's testimony.
Melos of the southwestern Cyclades — whose king Polyanax died as the heroes sailed home from Troy, and where Menestheus son of Peteos went to reign after leading the Athenians at Ilium.

Level Myconos of the Cyclades — where Thetis buried the Locrian Ajax son of Oileus after Athena wrecked his ship and Poseidon split the rock he clung to on the homeward voyage from Troy, and one of the isles that joined Minos when he mustered the Cyclades against Athens.
Andros of the northern Cyclades — the first landfall of Phidippus son of Thessalus and the Coans on their homeward voyage from Troy, before the wind drove them on to Cyprus.
Sea-girt Tenos — where Heracles slew the winged Argonauts Zetes and Calais and heaped earth over their tombs, and where Athena later wrecked much of the Greek fleet sailing home from Troy.

Ceos of the western Cyclades — where Aristaeus son of Apollo settled after Sirius scorched the Minoan isles, gathered the Parrhasian people of Lycaon's line, and built the great altar of Zeus Icmaeus on the mountains.

The mountain altar of Zeus Icmaeus on Ceos — where Aristaeus, at Apollo's command, offered sacrifice to Sirius and Zeus son of Cronus and so ended the plague that Sirius had brought upon the Minoan isles.
Kimolos of the chalky fields — the western Cycladic isle that agreed to aid Minos when he mustered the islands against Athens.

Level Seriphos — where Acrisius' chest bearing Danae and Perseus came ashore, Dictys the fisherman reared the hero, Polydectes sent him after the Gorgon's head, and Perseus returned to turn the king to stone and set Dictys on the throne.

Siphnos of the gold mines — whose island wealth built the treasury at Delphi until greed stopped the tithe and the sea flooded the workings; and home of Arne the impious Siphnian, who betrayed her city for gold and was changed to a black-foot daw.
Syros covered with wild thyme — a Cycladic isle that joined Minos' allies when he gathered the islands against Athens.
Parthenia of the Imbrasian Hera — the Ionian isle whose great sanctuary Apollonius names the seat of Hera, whence Poseidon's son Ancaeus sailed with Jason to Colchis.
Rhodes of the nymph Rhodos — Helios' beloved isle, where Tlepolemus son of Heracles settled in Lindos, Ialysus and Cameirus and led nine ships to Troy.
Cos of Eurypylus — the Dorian isle whose king Heracles stormed by night when the Coans took his ships for pirates, and whence the sons of Thessalus led island ships to Troy.
Calliste-Thera — the Cycladic isle Euphemus' clod raised from the sea, later renamed for Theras son of Autesion when he led the Minyan settlers from Sparta.
Sacred Cythera — the island Hesiod names where Aphrodite drifted ashore from the sea-foam before Cyprus, and past which Odysseus was driven when Malea beat him back.
Lesbos of the Aeolian migration — the North Aegean isle Penthilus son of Orestes seized when the Heracleidae drove the Pelopids from the mainland.
Salamis on Cyprus — the second city Teucer founded after Telamon drove him from his father's Attic isle, where the kings traced their descent through the daughter of Cinyras.
The Heraion of Samos — the great Ionian temple of Hera whose bronze statues of victors Pausanias saw standing in the goddess's precinct beside the Maeander's coast.
Didyma beside Miletus — Apollo's Ionian oracle where Pausanias marvelled at the colossal temple and Hyginus preserved the site among the god's prophetic seats.
Rhamnus of Attica — the coastal deme where Nemesis had her oldest cult, which Pausanias saw on the shore and Ovid named when the goddess of Rhamnus avenged mortal pride.
Sounion at the Cape — Poseidon's cliff-top sanctuary where Homer set the tomb of Phrontis and Pausanias saw the temple commanding the Saronic gulf.
Miletus on the Maeander's mouth — the Ionian citadel whence Erginus son of Poseidon sailed with the Argonauts, boasting his skill in seacraft and war.
Ephesus of Artemis — where Heracles bound the Cercopes in Omphale's service and where all cities, Pausanias says, worship Artemis of Ephesus above every other god.
Aea of Aeetes on the Phasis — the Colchian capital where Phrixus sacrificed the golden ram and Jason faced the brazen-footed bulls for the fleece.
Sardis beneath Tmolus — capital of Lydia, where Omphale held Heracles in servitude and Midas bathed away the golden touch in the river's snowy foam.
Halicarnassus on the Carian coast — city of Mausolus and Queen Artemisia, whose tomb Pausanias counted among the wonders of the world.
Dardanus on the Hellespont shore — the city Teucer son of Scamander shared with Dardanus before sacred Ilios rose in the plain and the kingdom took the younger founder's name.
Sinope on the Euxine — the Assyrian-shore colony where Zeus gave the nymph Sinope, daughter of Asopus, a home and the virginity she chose when he promised her heart's desire.
Pergamon above the Caicus — called of old Teuthrania, where Teuthras received Auge and Telephus succeeded to the Mysian throne after the Greeks mistook its coast for Troy.
Gordion on the Phrygian plateau — seat of Gordius and Midas, where Phrygian peasants brought strayed Silenus to the king who would judge Apollo's music on Tmolus.
Smyrna on the Aeolian coast — one of the twelve Aeolian cities on the site the Smyrnaeans still call the old town, before Ionian colonists from Colophon displaced the earlier settlers.

The same passage records that Ionians from Colophon seized Smyrna and later granted its people a seat at the Ionian assembly at Panionium — and elsewhere Pausanias calls the Smyrnaeans an Ionian people who drove the Lydians from their town.
Tarsus in Cilicia — whose river Cydnus Pausanias ranked among the coldest streams of the Greek world, refreshing to drink and to bathe in without winter's bite.
Cilicia on the southern coast of Asia Minor — the region Cilix son of Agenor settled when he abandoned the search for Europa and gave his name to the land and its people.
Phoenicia on the Syrian coast — Agenor's kingdom when Zeus bore Europa away, and the homeland his sons were forbidden to return to without her.
Side on the Pamphylian coast — whose river Melas Pausanias counted among the coldest waters of Asia Minor, and which Apollodorus lists among the cities Achilles ravaged before Troy.
Aeolian Cyme on the Asian coast — the city Hesiod left in poverty when he crossed the sea to settle near Helicon, and one of the western settlements the Cypria counts among Achilles' early conquests.
Xanthus by the eddying river — capital of Lycia whence Sarpedon and peerless Glaucus led their men to Troy, and where Bellerophon won his kingdom after slaying the Chimera in the hills above.

Patara of the Lycians — Apollo's coastal oracle that Ovid names with Claros and Delphi when the god walked among mortals, and where Pausanias saw a bronze bowl the Lycians said Telephus dedicated and Hephaestus made.
Corcyra the Black — Scheria of the Phaeacians, where Poseidon settled the nymph Corcyra, Alcinous ruled, Odysseus found harbour, and Arete married Jason to Medea.

Ogygia — the isle far off in the sea where the nymph Calypso kept Odysseus seven years in her hollow caves, yearning that he should be her husband, until Hermes bore Zeus' command that the hero must go free.
Apollodorus sends Odysseus there after the shipwreck: clinging to the mast of his wrecked vessel he was carried across the whirlpool to Calypso's island.

The isle of Aeaea, where fair-tressed Circe the dread goddess of human speech turned Odysseus' comrades to swine until Hermes gave the hero the herb moly and she bound herself by oath to restore them and send him on.

Homer makes Circe own sister to Aeetes of baneful mind — both sprung from Helius and Perse daughter of Ocean. Elpenor fell drunk from her roof; his shade begged burial before the company sailed for Hades. Apollodorus adds that Odysseus begot Telegonus on her, and that in one ending Telegonus returned here with Odysseus' corpse and Penelope after unknowingly killing his father on Ithaca.

Apollodorus sends the returning Argo to Aeaea after the murder of Apsyrtus: the ship itself spoke that Zeus' wrath would not cease until the crew were purified by Circe in Ausonia, and Jason and Medea supplicated her there before the voyage home continued.
Thrinacia, the isle where Helios kept seven herds of cattle and seven flocks of sheep — fifty in each, deathless and without offspring — guarded by his daughters Lampetie and Phaethusa.

Though Odysseus forbade it, hunger drove his crew to slaughter the sacred kine; Helios demanded vengeance from Zeus, the ship was shattered by a thunderbolt, and every companion perished — fulfilling the poem's charge that they destroyed their homecoming by devouring the cattle of Helios Hyperion.
Rocky Ithaca — furthest toward the gloom of the western isles, a rugged nurse of young men and the kingdom of Odysseus, Laertes, and Telemachus, besieged by suitors until the king's return.

Apollodorus assigns twelve wooers specifically from Ithaca itself — Antinous, Pronous, Liodes, Eurynomus, Amphimachus, Amphialus, Promachus, Amphimedon, Aristratus, Helenus, Dulicheus, and Ctesippus — beside the larger island contingents from Dulichium, Same, and Zacynthus.

The island catalogues over, Apollodorus tells how the wooers journeyed to Odysseus' palace and consumed his herds at their feasts, while Penelope held them off with the shroud of Laertes — weaving by day and undoing the web by night for three years until she was caught.

When the stratagem failed, she set before them Odysseus' bow — received long ago from Iphitus — and promised marriage to whoever could bend it; Odysseus strung the weapon, slew the suitors with Eumaeus, Philoetius, and Telemachus, hanged the faithless handmaids including Melantho, and made himself known to Penelope and Laertes — while Dolius and his sons, and the herald Medon spared by Telemachus, stood with the king at the last.
Same and the Cephallenian isles — the people who held forested Neriton and sailed under Odysseus in twelve ships to Troy, whom Laertes once ruled as lord of the Cephallenians.
Wooded Zacynthus — one of the western isles whose princes joined the suitors in Odysseus' halls and whose twenty youths Telemachus counted among the wooers' allies.
The white rock Leucas — passed by Hermes leading the suitors' ghosts down the dank ways toward Oceanus, the gates of the sun, and the land of dreams on the road to Hades.
Sacred Lemnos — isle of Thoas and Hypsipyle, where the Argonauts lay with the Lemnian women, Hephaestus fell from heaven, and Philoctetes was left with the bow of Heracles.
Chios of Oenopion — the Ionian isle where Orion wooed Merope and was blinded, and whence the hunter went to the sunrise to regain his sight.
Paros of the marble cliffs — held by the sons of Minos until Heracles slew them, and the place where Minos learned of Androgeus' death while sacrificing to the Graces.
Thasos of the north Aegean — where Heracles subjugated the Thracians and gave the isle to the sons of Androgeus, and where Cleoboea first brought Demeter's orgies from Paros.
Icaria — once called Doliche, renamed when Heracles buried the body of Icarus washed ashore; Dionysus later hired passage from here toward Naxos.
Scyros of King Lycomedes — the Sporades isle where Thetis hid Achilles as Pyrrha among the king's daughters, where Neoptolemus was born, and where Theseus was cast into the abyss.
Sciathus — the western gate of the Northern Sporades, where the Argo came in sight of the island as the heroes sped past Pelion toward the tomb of Dolops on the Magnesian shore.
Peparethos, rich in glossy olives — the Sporades isle whose name survives in Peparethus, son of Dionysus and Ariadne, and which the Cretan fleet of Minos passed without aid on the way to Oenopia.
Ikos, the easternmost of the Northern Sporades — ancient island in the Magnesian island chain where Sciathus and Peparethos lie on the Argonaut route.
Rocky Calydon of Oeneus — where Artemis loosed the white-tusked boar on the slighted harvest, and Meleager gathered heroes from many cities for the great hunt.
Steep Pleuron — sister city of Calydon in Aetolia, where Portheus' sons Agrius, Melas, and Oeneus dwelt, and where Thoas son of Andraemon ruled when the Aetolians sailed to Troy.

Dulichium — one of the western isles toward the dawn, where Phyleus made his dwelling in wrath against his father and whence his son Meges led forty ships; its princes also fed among the suitors of Penelope.
Amphilochian Argos — chief settlement of Acarnania west of the Achelous, where Alcmaeon and his sons Acarnan and Amphoterus led colonists from Epirus and gave the land its name.
Buthrotum in Chaonia — the Epirote city Helenus founded after Troy, a mimic Troy where the Trojan seer reigned and Aeneas found prophecy for the voyage west.

Cichyrus in Thesprotia — the inland Epirote city also called Ephyra, near the lake Acherusia and the rivers Acheron and Cocytus; Phylas was its king when Heracles took it, and Apollodorus makes it the kingdom Callidice offered Odysseus when he came through Epirus after sacrificing to Hades, Persephone, and Tiresias.
The oracle of the dead above the Acheron — where Pausanias believed Homer had walked before he sent Odysseus to dig the pit of blood and summon the shades from the house of Hades.

Ambracia on the Ambracian gulf — the Epirote city Aeneas passed after Ithaca and Samos, contended in Ovid's telling between disputing gods and famed thereafter for Actian Apollo; Hyginus says the bones of Neoptolemus were scattered through its land after Orestes slew him at Delphi.

Mantinea in Arcadia — founded when Antinoe daughter of Cepheus moved the city at a snake's guidance, with the river Ophis at its walls and the grave of Arcas beside Hera's altar, where the Mantineans set his bones brought from Maenalus at Delphi's command.

Apollodorus records a variant Odyssey ending in which Penelope, sent away by Odysseus after Antinous, came to Mantinea and bore Pan to Hermes; the Mantineans themselves told Pausanias that Odysseus cast Penelope out for paramours, that she went first to Lacedaemon and then died at Mantinea.
Campania of the Italian plain — where Apollodorus sends Philoctetes after Troy among the Campanians, in the same westward strand of myth that receives Aeneas and the exiled Diomedes.
Libya — the western land beyond the Greek map where Guneus son of Ocytus settled after Troy with the Aenianians and where Canthus the Argonaut perished while raiding flocks on the homeward voyage.
The well of Glauce at Corinth — where the bride, tricked into donning Medea's poisoned robe, ran to quench the burning fire that consumed her flesh and the palace of Creon.

name: Altar of Hera of the Height

summary.text: The altar of Hera Acraea on Corinth's height — where, in one strand of the Medea tale, the Colchian witch left her infant sons as suppliants before she fled on winged dragons after the murder of Glauce and Creon.
The Strophades isles off western Greece — where the sons of Boreas, Calais and Zetes, drove the Harpies from blind Phineus at the Argonauts' bidding.
Pellene in Achaea — whence Asterion son of Cometes sailed aboard the Argo, and one of the towns the heroes touched on their outward voyage.
Piresia in Thessaly — the town of Asterius son of Hyperbios, who joined Jason's crew from the Thessalian coast.
Pella on the Macedonian plain — later the royal seat of Philip and Alexander; in the heroic age a town of Emathia on the route between Thessaly and the north.
Troezen in the Argolid — Pittheus' kingdom where Aegeus lay with Aethra and Theseus was reared, and where Hippolytus worshipped Artemis before his death.

Hermione on the eastern Argive coast — where Apollodorus says Demeter learned from the Hermionians that Pluto had taken Persephone, and where Pausanias heard that Helen bore Iphigenia to Theseus and entrusted the child to Clytaemnestra to be reared as her own.
Marathon in eastern Attica — where Theseus killed the bull of Marathon on his road to Athens and later gave his name to the plain of the Athenian victory.
Colonus near Athens — the Attic deme sacred to Poseidon and the Eumenides, where blind Oedipus at last found refuge and a secret death at Theseus' side.
Aphidnae in northern Attica — one of the Attic demes where Theseus hid Helen after he carried her off from Sparta, before the Dioscuri recovered her.
Aulis on the Euripus — the Boeotian harbour where Agamemnon mustered the Achaean fleet for Troy and where Artemis demanded the sacrifice of Iphigenia before the winds would blow.
summary.citation: Iliad 2.303–329; Bibliotheca Epitome 3.21; Description of Greece 9.19.6

summary.text: Pisa in Elis — Pelops' kingdom beside Olympia, where he won Hippodamia in the chariot race against Oenomaus and founded the line that ruled the Peloponnese.
Azania in Arcadia — the district Arcas named for his son Azan when he divided the land, whence Cleitor son of Azan came to be the most powerful of the Arcadian kings.
Tegea in Arcadia — Aleus' ancient city, home of Atalanta and Auge, where Telephus was born and where Agapenor led the Arcadian host to Troy.
Glisas in Boeotia — a town on the road from Thebes where the Epigoni first joined battle before they marched against the seven-gated city.
Messene in the western Peloponnese — kingdom of Aphareus and Leucippus, home of the Apharetids Idas and Lynceus, and later allotted to the Heraclid Cresphontes.
Panopeus in Phocis — the city of Epeius the carpenter, builder of the wooden horse, and of the Phocian chiefs who sailed for Troy.
summary.citation: Iliad 2.517; Bibliotheca Epitome 5.14; Description of Greece 10.4.1

summary.text: Psophis in Arcadia — where Alcmaeon fled after matricide, married Arsinoe and Callirrhoe, and was buried beside the river Aroanius.

Phylace in Phthiotis — citadel of warlike Protesilaus in the Catalogue of Ships, first of the Achaeans to leap ashore at Troy; his widow Laodamia was left wailing here when the black earth already held him fast.
Amydon on the Axios — Paeonian polis in Agamemnon's muster roll, whence Pyraechmes and Asteropaeus led their spearmen to the plain of Troy.
Colophon on the Ionian coast — city of Calchas the seer and Mopsus, where the Lapith chiefs and Podalirius mustered for Troy and where Arachne's contest with Athena was set.
Cyzicus on the Propontis — city of the Doliones where King Cyzicus welcomed the Argonauts at harbour and was slain by Jason in a night of mistaken battle.
Thespiae in Boeotia — city beneath Helicon where Heracles met the Muses and where the Boeotian chiefs who sailed for Troy held their muster in Homer's Catalogue of Ships.
The far kingdom of Cepheus and Cassiopeia — where Andromeda was chained to the rock until Perseus flew down on winged sandals and won her from the sea-monster.
Plataea on the Asopus — Boeotian ally of Athens in myth and history, and in the Catalogue of Ships the polis whose chiefs sailed under the sons of Asopus for Troy.
Schoenus in Boeotia — a polis in Homer's Catalogue of Ships and the legendary home of Schoeneus, father of Atalanta in the hunt for the Calydonian boar.
Eleon in Boeotia — one of the lesser Boeotian poleis in the Catalogue of Ships, whose chiefs sailed with Leitus and Peneleos for the plain of Troy.
Sicyon in the Corinthian plain — ancient kingdom of Epopeus and Adrastus, where Pelops' line first held sway before the Argive kings, and a polis in Agamemnon's muster roll.
The flowery isle of the Sirens — where Orpheus drowned their song with his lyre on the Argonaut voyage and where Odysseus later had his crew stop their ears with wax.
Anthedon on the Euboean strait — Boeotian harbour town where the fisherman Glaucus became a sea-god after eating the grass of immortality, and a polis in the Catalogue of Ships.
Percote on the Hellespont shore — pasture of Merops the seer, whose sons Adrastus and Amphius fell at Troy, and a Trojan settlement in Homer's catalogue of allies.
Tenedos off the Troad coast — island where the Achaeans feigned retreat and hid their fleet behind the headland before the sack of Troy, and where Neoptolemus paused on his voyage home.
summary.citation: Odyssey 3.169–172; Bibliotheca Epitome 5.19–20; Description of Greece 10.14.2

summary.text: Lyctus on Crete — one of the hundred-citied island's towns whose warriors followed Idomeneus and Meriones to Troy in Homer's Catalogue of Ships.
Rhytium, well-peopled among other towns — the Cretan city named beside Lyctus whose spearmen sailed under Idomeneus for the war at Ilion.
Antandros beneath Ida — the Troad city whence Aeneas fled the burning of Troy with his son Ascanius, carrying the household gods toward the western sea.
Chryse on the Troad — Apollo's shrine beside the sea where the priest Chryses restored his daughter and the god stayed the plague upon the Greek host.
Magnesia on the Pagasaean coast — the Thessalian region whence Hyginus names Phocus and Priasus, sons of Caeneus, among Jason's Argonauts.
Homer's Catalogue of Ships sets the Magnetes about the fair-flowing Peneius and forested Pelion — forty black ships under swift Prothous son of Tenthredon.
Meliboea in Magnesia — a coastal town of the Catalogue whose bowmen followed Philoctetes in seven companies from the Pagasaean shore.
Methone in Magnesia — the well-built city whose bowmen followed Philoctetes in seven companies from the Pagasaean shore in the muster of the Achaean kings.
Olizon on the Magnesian coast — Philoctetes' city, whence the archer of Heracles sailed for Troy before the serpent's bite left him on Lemnos.
Pharos off Egypt — the isle where Menelaus was wind-bound until Eidothea sent him to wrest counsel from her father Proteus the Old Man of the Sea.
Thaumacia in Magnesia — one of the towns beside Olizon and Methone whose bowmen followed Philoctetes to the war at Troy.
Abdera in Thrace — the city Heracles founded beside the Nestos in memory of his companion Abderus, devoured by the mares of Diomedes.
Bistonia in Thrace — kingdom of Diomedes son of Ares, king of the warlike Bistones who kept man-eating mares; Heracles slew him there and founded Abdera beside the grave of Abderus.
Adramyttium in Mysia — the Aeolian city whose plain Achilles ravaged on the way to Troy, in the Cypria's account of the first Greek landings in Asia.
The floating isle of Aeolus — where the keeper of the winds entertained Odysseus and sealed the storm-blasts in a bull's hide bag for the voyage home.
Alybe, land of silver — the far Pontic country of the Halizones whose warriors followed Odius and Epistrophus in Homer's Catalogue of Ships.

Abydus on the Asiatic shore of the Hellespont — one of the settlements mustered by Asius son of Hyrtacus from Arisbe beside the Selleïs, and the home Priam's bastard Democoon left when he came to aid the Trojans.
Adrasteia in the Troad — city of Adrastus and Amphius, sons of Merops the seer of Percote, whom even their father's prophecies could not keep from sailing to Troy.
Aenus at the mouth of the Hebrus — Thracian city whence Peiros son of Imbrasus came to cast the stone that crushed Odysseus' comrade in the press of battle before Troy.
Alope in Phthiotis — Pelasgian settlement in the Myrmidons' muster, home of Peleus and the land from which Achilles led fifty ships when yet he raged withdrawn from battle.
Amathus on Cyprus — metal-rich city whose Propoetides denied Aphrodite and were turned to stone, the shame that drove Pygmalion to carve his ivory bride.
Amyclae in Laconia — ancient neighbour of Sparta in Menelaus' kingdom, a citadel hard by the sea in the Catalogue of Ships and the place where Cassandra met her doom after the fall of Troy.
Anemoreia in Phocis — windy height above the Cephisus valley in the Catalogue of Ships, whence Schedius and Epistrophus led the Phocian host.
Antron on the Phthiotian coast — polis in Protesilaus' contingent, whose captain was the first Achaean to leap ashore at Troy and the first to fall.
Apaesus in the Troad — neighbour of Adrasteia and Pityeia, held by Adrastus and Amphius the linen-corsleted sons of Merops of Percote.
Arisbe on the Selleïs — whence Asius son of Hyrtacus drove his tawny horses to lead Percote, Practius, Sestus, and Abydus against the Achaeans.
Arne in Boeotia — vine-rich polis in the fifty-ship Boeotian muster whose warriors followed Peneleos, Leitus, and the captains of the Minyan plain.
Arne in the Troad — a Hellespontine settlement homonymous with the vine-rich Boeotian city, in the hinterland of Adrasteia and Apaesus attested in the ancient gazetteers.
Ascania far inland — Phrygian country whence Phorcys and godlike Ascanius led their contingent to Troy beneath Mount Tmolus.
Aspledon in Boeotia — Minyan town whose warriors Ascalaphus and Ialmenus, sons of Ares by Astyoche, led to Troy.
Carystus on southern Euboea — stronghold of the long-haired Abantes who followed Elephenor son of Chalcodon against Troy.
Ciconia in Thrace — tribal land beside Ismarus whence Euphemus led Ciconian spearmen to Troy and where Odysseus first sacked a city on his way home from Ilios.
Copae on Lake Copais — Boeotian town whose men marched in the fifty ships beside Medeon and the well-built citadel.
Coroneia in Boeotia — polis in the fifty-ship muster with a sanctuary of Itonian Athena where the Boeotian confederacy gathered.
Sacred Crisa in Phocis — Homeric name for the Delphic port town later called Cirrha, named beside rocky Pytho when Schedius and Epistrophus mustered the forty Phocian ships.
Cromna on the Paphlagonian coast — Eneti town beside Cytorus and Sesamon in the cluster Pylaemenes held when he marshalled the shaggy-hearted Paphlagonians for Troy.
Cyclopes' Isle off Sicily — the rugged shore where Odysseus and his companions blinded Polyphemus son of Poseidon after the Cyclops devoured several of the Ithacans.
Cyparissus in Phocis — interior town beside rocky Pytho in the Catalogue of Ships when Schedius and Epistrophus led the forty Phocian ships; homonym-safe id distinct from the Ceos youth of Apollo.
Cyphus in Perrhaebian Thessaly — town whence Gouneus led twenty-two ships with the Enienes and Peraebi, whose dwellings Homer sets about wintry Dodona and the ploughland by lovely Titaressus.
Cytorus on the Paphlagonian coast — Eneti town Pylaemenes held beside Sesamon, Cromna, Aegialus, and the river Parthenius when he marshalled the Paphlagonians for Troy.

Daulis on Parnassus — Phocian city where Pausanias places Tereus' kingdom, the pollution of the dining-table when Procne served Itys, and the sanctuary of Athena whose image the Daulians said Procne brought from Athens.
Edonia in Thrace — wine-rich country of the Edonians beside the Strymon, homeland of King Rhesus and the scene of Lycurgus son of Dryas who drove Dionysus into the sea.
Eilesion in Boeotia — polis that Homer names beside Harma and Erythrae in the Catalogue of Ships.
Erythrae at the foot of Cithaeron — Boeotian border town that Homer names beside Eilesium in the Catalogue of Ships; homonym-safe id distinct from the Ionian city on the coast of Asia.
Eteonus in Boeotia — ridge-crowned settlement that Homer names beside Scolus in the Catalogue of Ships, where tradition placed the burial of Oedipus in a sanctuary of Demeter.
Eutresis in Boeotia — settlement that Homer names beside Copae and dove-haunted Thisbe in the Catalogue of Ships; homonym-safe id distinct from Arcadian Eutresis.
Graia — the Boeotian polis that Homer names beside Thespiae and spacious Mycalessus in the Catalogue of Ships; homonym-safe id distinct from the early Euboean town near Eretria.
Gyrton in Perrhaebian Thessaly — the Lapith town beside Argissa, Orthe, Elone, and white Oloösson whence Polypoetes and Leonteus followed forty black ships to Troy; home of Coronus son of Caeneus.
Argissa in Perrhaebian Thessaly — Lapith town beside Gyrtone, Orthe, Elone, and white Oloösson whence Polypoetes and Leonteus ranged forty black ships to Troy.
Orthe in Perrhaebian Thessaly — Lapith settlement in the Catalogue of Ships beside Argissa and Gyrtone, whose spearmen followed Polypoetes and Leonteus to Troy.
Elone in Perrhaebian Thessaly — Lapith town named beside Argissa, Gyrtone, and Orthe in the Catalogue of Ships when Polypoetes and Leonteus led forty ships to Troy.
White Oloösson in Perrhaebian Thessaly — the Lapith polis Homer sets beside Argissa, Gyrtone, Orthe, and Elone whence Polypoetes and Leonteus followed forty black ships to Troy.
Haliartus — the grassy Boeotian town inland from Thespiae in Homer's Catalogue of Ships, where Pausanias saw the tomb of Lysander and the sanctuary of the Praxidicae beside Mount Tilphusius.

Halus in Achaea Phthiotis — coastal polis of the Myrmidons beside Alope and Trachis in Homer's Catalogue of Ships, one of the Phthiotian settlements from which Peleus and Achilles drew their fifty black ships.
Harma — the Boeotian polis that Homer names beside Mycalessus and Eilesium in the Catalogue of Ships, on the road between Tanagra and Thebes.

Hyampolis — the inland Phocian city whence the Hyantes fled from Cadmus and Boeotia, named in the Catalogue of Ships among the poleis about which Schedius and Epistrophus marshalled the forty black ships beside Anemoreia and the goodly river Cephisus.
Hyle — the Boeotian town on Lake Hylica that Homer names beside Eleon and Peteon when the fifty ships mustered; homonym-safe id distinct from Skapte Hyle in Thrace and other Hylic toponyms.
Hypaepa — the Lydian town beneath Tmolus where Arachne dwelt and where Pan boasted his reeds against Apollo's lyre before Midas judged the contest.

Hypata in the Spercheius valley — chief town of the Aenianes at the foot of Mount Oeta, whence Apollodorus' Guneus son of Ocytus led twenty-two ships of the Aenianians to Troy; Homer sets the Enienes' dwellings about wintry Dodona and the ploughland by lovely Titaressus in the same muster roll.
Hyria — the Boeotian polis that Homer names beside rocky Aulis and Schoenus in the Catalogue of Ships; homonym-safe id distinct from Hyria in Cilicia.
Iton — the mother-of-flocks polis in Phthiotis whence Protesilaus led forty black ships to Troy, first of the Achaeans to leap ashore at Ilion.
Telepylus of the Laestrygonians — the lofty citadel where Antiphates' people drove rocks from the cliffs and destroyed all Odysseus' ships save his own black vessel.

Lebadeia in Boeotia — where Pausanias saw Trophonius' chthonic oracle beside the river Hercyna, the pit into which seekers descended after drinking from Lethe and Mnemosyne, and the treasury Agamedes and Trophonius built for Hyrieus.
Lerna — the marsh of Argolis where Heracles destroyed the many-headed Hydra with Iolaus' help, searing each neck with fire; Hera had nourished the beast in anger against the son of Zeus.
Leuctra on the Laconian coast — where Pausanias saw a temple and image of Cassandra under the local name Alexandra, with Athena on the acropolis and a grove of Eros beside the winter stream.
Lilaea at the sources of the Cephisus — Phocian polis in the Catalogue of Ships whose spears followed Schedius and Epistrophus beside Anemoreia and Hyampolis.
Lilybaeum on western Sicily — the harbour town where Orpheus' song held the Argonauts' oars still as they passed the island on the voyage east.
Land of the Lotus-eaters — the shore where Odysseus' scouts ate the honey-sweet lotus fruit and forgot Ithaca until he dragged them weeping back to the ships.
Lyrnessus on the Troad — sacked by Achilles beside Thebe Hypoplakia, whose captive Briseïs became the prize that kindled the quarrel with Agamemnon.
Maroneia in Thrace — where Apollo's priest Maron gave Odysseus the potent wine that stupefied Polyphemus when the Ithacans blinded the Cyclops.
Medeon — the well-built Boeotian citadel in the Catalogue of Ships whose chiefs sailed with Leitus and Peneleos for the plain of Troy.
Mycalessus — the broad Boeotian town in the Catalogue of Ships whose spearmen followed the fifty-ship muster under Leitus and Peneleos.
Notium on the Ionian coast — the harbour where Calchas the seer died after leaving Troy, and where Amphilochus and the Lapith chiefs held their muster in the Catalogue of Ships.
Ocalea in Boeotia — one of the lesser poleis in the Catalogue of Ships whose chiefs sailed with Leitus and Peneleos for Troy.

Oechalia in Malis — city of archer-king Eurytus, named with Tricca and Ithome in the Catalogue of Ships as one of the poleis whose levies Machaon and Podalirius commanded, and the city Heracles sacked for Iole after Eurytus refused him in marriage.
Onchestus — Poseidon's holy grove in Boeotia, named in the Catalogue of Ships beside the lesser poleis whose fifty ships mustered under Leitus and Peneleos.
Opus in Opuntian Locris — homeland of Oileus and the Locrian Ajax, and the city whose spears followed Patroclus' father Menoetius in Agamemnon's muster.
Ormenion in Magnesia — the Ormenian settlement beside the fountain Hypereia, Asterium, and the white crests of Titanus whence Eurypylus son of Euaemon led forty black ships to the plain of Troy.
Pagasae on the Magnesian coast — the harbour of Iolcus where Jason assembled the Argonauts and the Argo first put to sea on the quest for the Golden Fleece.
Pieria beneath Olympus' north face — where Hermes drove Apollo's cattle from the pasture of Neleus and Battus the forester betrayed his oath and was turned to touchstone.
Doris over against the Peloponnese — the country Hellen's son Dorus received in the tripartite division of Hellas and named after himself.
Peteon in Boeotia — Boeotian polis in the Catalogue of Ships beside Hyle and Eleon, whose chiefs sailed with Leitus and Peneleos for Troy.
Phlius in Corinthia — city of Asopus and the Phliantids, whose king Aras gave his name to the land; Heracles took it in war and gave the kingdom to Phlius son of Dionysus and Ariadne.
Stenyclarus in Messenia — city of the Heraclid Cresphontes, who drew the lot for the Peloponnese and reigned here until he was murdered by Polyphontes.
Tauris on the Scythian coast — land of the Taurians where Artemis received human sacrifice and where Iphigenia served as priestess until Orestes and Pylades came to steal her image.
Phaestus on Crete's southern plain — Minoan city beside the Libyan sea, where Rhadamanthys held sway and where Telephus son of Heracles was reared among the Cretans.
Trachis in Malis — coastal kingdom of Ceyx and the home Heracles chose beside the Malian gulf, where Deianira sent the poisoned robe and where Peleus and Achilles dwelt before Troy.
Tamassos in Cyprus — inland city of the copper country, where Atalanta's suitors ran for the bride and where the Cypriot kings held their wealth in the island's heart.
Pteleos in Phthiotis — Phthiotic polis in the Catalogue of Ships whence Protesilaus led forty black ships to be first ashore at Troy and first to die.
Pyrasus in Phthiotis — Phthiotic settlement beside the gulf in the Catalogue of Ships, whose spearmen followed Protesilaus and Podarces to the plain of Troy.
Salmydessus on the Thracian coast — bitter shore where Phineus the seer was tormented by the Harpies until Zetes and Calais drove them off on the Argonauts' voyage.
Stymphalus in Arcadia — city beside the lake where Heracles drove off the man-eating birds with brazen beaks and where the eponym Stymphalus son of Elatus ruled.

Cleitor on the northern Arcadian plain — the city Cleitor son of Azan founded and named after himself, ringed by low hills with sanctuaries of Demeter, Asclepius, and Eileithyia still standing in Pausanias' day.
Lycosura on Mount Lycaeus — the city Lycaon founded, which Pausanias calls the oldest on earth, seat of Cleitor son of Azan and cradle of the Lycaean cult of Zeus.
Pholoe in Arcadia — mountain and woodland of the centaur Pholus, where Heracles hunted the Erymanthian boar and where the guest opened the jar of wine that drew the centaurs to battle.
Sigeum on the Hellespont — promontory at the mouth of the Scamander where Achilles' tomb stood and where the Trojans burned Polyxena at the hero's barrow after the war.
summary.citation: Iliad 24.349–353; Bibliotheca Epitome 5.23; Description of Greece 10.24.5

summary.text: Rhoeteum on the Trojan coast — headland where the Aegean meets the Hellespont and where Ajax son of Telamon was buried after he flung himself on his sword.
summary.citation: Iliad 2.841–842; Bibliotheca Epitome 5.6; Description of Greece 1.35.3

summary.text: Thebe under Placus in the Troad — city of Eetion the Mysian, father of Andromache, whom Achilles sacked beside the wooded slopes of Mount Placus.
Zeleia on the Aesepus — Lycian settlement in the Troad whence Pandarus son of Lycaon led the archers who broke the truce with an arrow at Menelaus.
Sestus on the Hellespont — Thracian city on the European shore opposite Abydus, whence Asius son of Hyrtacus led his horses to the plain of Troy.
Practius on the Asian shore — settlement beside the Practius river in the Troad, homeland of Asius son of Hyrtacus and his Trojan spearmen.
Pityeia in the Troad — city of Merops the seer, whose sons Adrastus and Amphius marched to Troy though their father forbade them.
Tereia in the Troad — settlement of Merops the seer on the Asian coast, whence Adrastus and Amphius sailed with the Trojan allies.
Sesamon in Paphlagonia — coastal city whence Pylaemenes led the Paphlagonian shields to Troy and where his son Harpalion fell on the plain.
Steiria in Attica — deme on the east coast whence Peteus son of Orneus ruled and Menestheus marshalled the Athenian host for Troy.
Stiris in Phocis — Phocian polis whose name Peteus brought to Attica when he fled the wrath of his father and settled at Steiria.
Thisbe in Boeotia — Boeotian polis in the Catalogue of Ships beside Scolus and Potniae, whose chiefs sailed with Leitus and Peneleos for Troy.
Scolus in Boeotia — Boeotian settlement in the Catalogue of Ships whose warriors followed the captains of the Boeotian contingent to Ilion.
Potniae in Boeotia — city sacred to Dionysus Potniaeus in the Catalogue of Ships, whose spearmen sailed with the Boeotian lords for Troy.
Ithome of the crags in Histiaeotis — Homer's stepped citadel west of Tricca, one of the three Thessalian poleis whose levies Machaon and Podalirius commanded in the Catalogue of Ships.
Tricca in Thessaly — with Ithome of the crags and Oechalia, city of Eurytus, one of the three poleis whose thirty hollow ships Machaon and Podalirius, sons of Asclepius, led to Troy.
Styra on Euboea — Abantian city whence Elephenor led the Euboean spears to Troy and where Chalcodon son of Abas ruled before the war.
Gargaphie on Cithaeron — vale of cypress sacred to Artemis, where Actaeon stumbled on the goddess bathing and was turned to a stag for his own hounds to run down.
Taenarus in Laconia — cape where an cave opened to the land of the dead, through which Orpheus descended for Eurydice and Theseus with Peirithous sought Persephone.
Thermopylae in Malis — narrow pass between mountain and sea beside Trachis, where Ceyx the seaborn king ruled and where the Malian gulf meets the foothills of Oeta.
Sardinia at the western horizon — island where Aristaeus fled after Actaeon's death and where Pausanias sends the son of Apollo to consult the nymphs.
Illyria of the Encheleans — land of exile where Cadmus and Harmonia led the tribe against the Illyrians and were at last transformed into serpents with crested backs.
